migrationNotes: Spine: we shrink down and travel into a cell from the outside, passing its boundary and then each thing inside it in turn.
Each stop is a part with a job (boundary, DNA store, power station, light catcher, wall), and the parts we meet let us sort cells into kinds.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-inside-a-cell-hook, -nucleus-check, -dna-why, -organelle-check. Their meaning is covered by other items.

lesson.title: A world inside a cell

lead.text: We begin outside, at the surface of one cell. Whatever its shape, a cell is a small bag of watery living material, and the bag is never shut off from the world. Food and oxygen have to get in, and waste has to get out, all day long.

Something in the skin of the bag has to decide what goes where. A skin that sealed the cell would starve it and trap its own waste. A skin with no control at all would let the contents drift out and the cell's chemistry fall apart. Every cell has a thin layer that sits between those extremes, called the plasma membrane or cell membrane. It acts like a doorkeeper, letting some substances through and holding others back.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows one edge doing three jobs: letting food and oxygen in, letting waste out and turning other particles away. Every living cell is wrapped in a plasma membrane like this. Everything we meet from here on lies inside it. The first thing to find there is the cell's store of instructions.

lead.text: Think back to the edge of the animal cell and of the bacterium.

Inside the membrane, the first thing to find is the cell's instructions. Every cell carries a complete set, written in a long molecule called DNA, and it uses them to build its parts and to make copies of itself. Where a cell keeps that molecule is the clearest way to tell one kind of cell from another.

Animal cells and plant cells are eukaryotic (say yoo-KARR-ee-OT-ik). In a eukaryotic cell most of the DNA sits inside a nucleus, a compartment with a membrane of its own. A good picture is a locked office in the middle of a busy workshop. The master plans stay safe in one place, away from the noise and the chemistry going on outside. Find the nucleus in the picture of the animal cell.

afterFigure.text: Now switch to the bacterium. A bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid, with no membrane round it, more like plans pinned to the wall of one open room. The DNA does the same job, and it simply isn't shut away.

So you can sort cells into two kinds by looking at where the DNA sits. If it sits behind a membrane of its own, in a nucleus, the cell is eukaryotic. If it lies in a nucleoid, the cell is a bacterium. Eukaryotic cells also contain other compartments, and those are the next stop.

lead.text: A bacterium still has instructions to store, but it has no compartment to store them in.

steps.headline: The working parts of a eukaryotic cell

lead.text: The nucleus is only one of several parts packed into a eukaryotic cell, and the parts are not interchangeable. Each is built for one job, and a part like that is called an organelle, which means 'little organ'. A cell works rather like a workshop with separate rooms, each set up for one task.

The first room to know is the power station. Mitochondria (one is a mitochondrion) take the energy stored in fuel such as sugar and hand it over in a form the cell can spend. A cell that spends a lot of energy, like a muscle cell, is packed with them. Find the mitochondria in the picture to see where they sit.

afterFigure.text: Then there are the ribosomes, tiny benches where the cell builds proteins by following instructions copied from its DNA. Proteins are the molecules that do most of the cell's work, from building its parts to speeding up its chemistry. Ribosomes are so basic that bacteria have them too. A bacterium has no mitochondria, though, because it has no compartments with membranes of their own.
An animal cell has all of these. A leaf cell has one more organelle, and that is the next stop.

lead.text: Now move from the animal cell to a leaf. A leaf cell has everything the animal cell has, plus chloroplasts. A chloroplast is an organelle that catches light energy, and it holds the green colouring that makes leaves green. The cell uses the energy it catches to make sugar. Find the chloroplasts in the picture of the leaf cell, then switch to the animal cell and look for them there.

afterFigure.text: Chloroplasts need light to work, and light does not reach every part of a plant. A cell in a root lives in dark soil and has none. It stays alive on sugar made in the leaves and sent down to it, and it still has mitochondria to release the energy from that sugar.
A leaf cell carries two organelles that deal with energy. One catches light and the other works on fuel. That raises a puzzle about what the cell does when the light goes out.

lead.text: Night falls over the leaf, and no light reaches its cells.

That completes the tour inside, so the last stop is back at the surface of the leaf cell. Outside its plasma membrane a plant cell has one more layer, the cell wall. It is a stiff, tough shell. Think of a water balloon sitting inside a cardboard box: the balloon can swell only until it presses against the box. In the picture the wall is the dashed outline round the plasma membrane.

afterFigure.text: The wall is full of gaps, so water and dissolved substances pass through it easily. It gives the cell a fixed shape, and it leaves the control of what enters and leaves to the plasma membrane inside it.

Plant cells are not the only ones that build a wall. Most bacteria have one as well, although the bacterium drawn earlier leaves it out to keep the picture simple. A wall by itself doesn't show that a cell is eukaryotic, whereas a nucleus does.

lead.text: Plants have no skeleton, yet a leaf stands up.

lesson.orientation: Connect cell structures to their jobs and distinguish bacteria from eukaryotes.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A drop of pond water under a microscope is crowded. Specks drift and swim through it, and some of them are green. Many of the specks are single cells, and each one is alive in the same ways you are. It takes in food and gets rid of waste, and it carries a complete set of instructions for building more of itself.

All of that happens inside a bag far too small to see. Dozens of animal cells would fit side by side across the head of a pin, and a bacterium is smaller still. Yet the bag has structure. Its edge controls what comes and goes, and inside it the parts have separate jobs, a little like a workshop with a locked office and a row of benches.
This lesson goes inside. We start at the cell's edge and move inwards one stop at a time. Each stop is a part with a job, and the parts we find let us tell one kind of cell from another.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a bacterium from an animal or plant cell, and say what each main part is for.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea in biology happens inside these cells.

recap.keyIdea: Every cell has a plasma membrane. Eukaryotic cells also have a nucleus and organelles with jobs, while a bacterium keeps its DNA in a nucleoid.

blocks.text: Back at the drop of pond water, each speck now has parts you can name. You named the plasma membrane every cell shares, worked out where a bacterium keeps its DNA, and decided which organelle keeps a leaf cell going after dark.

recap.nextHook: Everything a cell takes in or lets out has to cross its membrane, and the next lesson starts with two rooms and an open door to show which way a crowd of particles drifts.

questions.prompt: Both cells need food in and waste out. Name the structure around each cell that controls this exchange.
hints: Look at the outline of each cell.
Which layer acts as the doorkeeper, deciding what crosses?
Both cells share this structure, so it cannot be something only one of them has.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both cells exchange substances across a plasma membrane.

questions.onCorrect: The plasma membrane. Every cell has one, and it controls what enters and leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: A cell wall is an extra layer outside the boundary that some cells have. The boundary every cell has lies inside it.
You have the right kind of structure. Give its full name, as it appears on the first screen.
You have described where it is. The question asks for the structure's name.

questions.prompt: A bacterium has no nucleus. In which region of the cell does its DNA lie?
hints: Having no nucleus doesn't mean having no DNA.
Think of plans pinned to the wall of one open room, not locked in an office.
The region's name resembles the name of the compartment this cell lacks.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bacterial nucleoid holds DNA without a surrounding nuclear membrane.

questions.onCorrect: In the nucleoid. A bacterium has DNA, but no membrane wraps it.

misconceptions.feedback: Every cell has DNA. The bacterium just keeps it without a nuclear membrane.
A bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA lies in a region with a different name.
That describes it fairly, but the question asks for the name of the region where the DNA gathers.

questions.prompt: Leaf cells capture light, but after dark they still need energy from fuel. Which organelle does that job?
hints: Which organelle works with the energy stored in fuel?
Does that organelle need light to do its job?
A root cell, which sits in the dark soil, has it too.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells have chloroplasts for light and mitochondria for energy from fuel.

questions.onCorrect: Mitochondria. A leaf cell has both organelles because it does both jobs.

misconceptions.feedback: Chloroplasts need light. The job here goes on in the dark.
Ribosomes build proteins. Look for the organelle that works on fuel.

questions.prompt: Name the structure outside a plant cell's membrane that helps the cell hold its shape.
hints: Think back to the water balloon inside a cardboard box.
Look at the outermost layer of the leaf cell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cell wall gives external support; the membrane remains inside it.

questions.onCorrect: The cell wall. It props the cell up from outside and leaves the membrane in charge of exchange.

misconceptions.feedback: The membrane lies inside this layer. Name the structure outside it.

questions.prompt: A root cell is alive but has no chloroplasts. Which conclusion follows?
hints: Think about where roots are and what they do.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many plant cells, including root cells, have no chloroplasts and use sugars made elsewhere.

choices.label: It cannot be a plant cell
It cannot release energy from fuel

questions.onCorrect: Not every plant cell photosynthesises. Root cells use sugars made by the leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: Plant cells are defined by more than chloroplasts. Roots are plant tissue.
Releasing energy from fuel is the mitochondria's job, and root cells have those.

questions.prompt: Name the structure whose presence most directly shows that a cell is eukaryotic.
hints: Pick the distinctive structure, not one every cell shares.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane-bound nucleus distinguishes eukaryotic cells from bacterial cells.

questions.onCorrect: A nucleus. A plasma membrane is shared by all cells, so it can't tell the two types apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Bacteria have these too. Choose a structure bacteria lack.

questions.prompt: A cell has a plasma membrane and DNA, but no nucleus and no mitochondria. What kind of cell is it?
hints: Which cell type keeps its DNA in a nucleoid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No nucleus and no organelles is the bacterial design.

questions.onCorrect: A bacterium. No nucleus and no mitochondria is the bacterial design.

misconceptions.feedback: Animal and plant cells have a nucleus and mitochondria. This cell has neither.

questions.prompt: What should a cell's outer boundary be like?
hints: What would happen to the food if nothing could get in?

acceptedIdeas: A skin that lets some things through and keeps others out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A cell needs a boundary that lets some things through and keeps others out.

choices.label: A sealed wall that lets nothing through
A skin that lets some things through and keeps others out
No boundary, so the cell mixes with its surroundings

questions.onCorrect: A boundary that lets some things through and holds others back. Cells have exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: A sealed wall would starve the cell and trap its waste.
Without a boundary the cell's contents would drift away and its chemistry would fall apart.

questions.prompt: A cell keeps its DNA inside a nucleus. What kind of cell is it?
hints: Animal and plant cells are this kind.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A cell with a nucleus is eukaryotic.

questions.onCorrect: Eukaryotic. A nucleus holding the DNA is the mark of a eukaryotic cell.

misconceptions.feedback: Bacteria have no nucleus. Look for the cell type that does.

questions.prompt: What does the nucleus's own membrane do for the DNA?
hints: Think about what a membrane does for any compartment.

acceptedIdeas: It keeps most of the DNA enclosed in one compartment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nuclear membrane encloses most of the DNA in one compartment.

choices.label: It keeps most of the DNA enclosed in one compartment
It makes the DNA copy itself faster
It turns the DNA into protein

questions.onCorrect: It encloses the DNA. A membrane-bound compartment is what makes a nucleus a nucleus.

misconceptions.feedback: Copying is done by enzymes. The membrane's job is to enclose.
Proteins are built elsewhere in the cell. The nucleus holds the DNA that carries their instructions.

questions.prompt: Which organelle captures light energy in a leaf cell?
hints: Leaf cells are green because of it.
questions.onCorrect: The chloroplast. It captures light energy for photosynthesis.

misconceptions.feedback: Mitochondria work with fuel, not light.

Eukaryotic cells keep most DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus; bacteria have no nucleus and keep DNA in a nucleoid.
A bacterium has DNA in a nucleoid region without a surrounding nuclear membrane.
Eukaryotic organelles have jobs: mitochondria transfer energy from fuel and ribosomes make proteins; bacteria have ribosomes but no mitochondria.
Leaf cells have chloroplasts, which capture light energy, and mitochondria; cells that receive no light, such as root cells, have no chloroplasts.
Photosynthetic leaf cells have chloroplasts for light capture and mitochondria for energy transfer from fuel.
A plant cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and helps resist expansion; many bacteria also have a wall.
A plant cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and helps the cell resist expansion and keep its shape.
The nucleus encloses most of the cell's DNA.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; mitochondria serve a different energy role.
Both cells exchange substances across a plasma membrane.
A bacterial nucleoid holds DNA without a surrounding nuclear membrane.
Leaf cells have chloroplasts for light and mitochondria for energy from fuel.
The cell wall gives external support; the membrane remains inside it.
Many plant cells, including root cells, have no chloroplasts and use sugars made elsewhere.
A membrane-bound nucleus distinguishes eukaryotic cells from bacterial cells.
No nucleus and no organelles is the bacterial design.
